endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: (ii) ensures the mental health chatbot is developed and monitored in a manner 252 consistent with clinical best practices;

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is essential to be transparent about the intended population and purpose of risk models, such as the AE risk model, for end users and patients.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: i) En tities, e.g., AI developers, should make information available about the intended use of generative AI in health care and identify the purpose of its use.

endorsements.title: Generative artificial intelligence in posttraumatic stress disorder treatment: Exploring five different use cases
endorsements.quote: Users should be explicitly made aware of the intended use and the known limitations of the available tools (e.g., no real‐time monitoring by human clinicians, inability to perform crisis intervention).

endorsements.title: Conversational AI for perinatal mental health: promise, limits, and a human-AI stepped-care framework
endorsements.quote: For that reason, digital doulas should be designed with conservative escalation thresholds, transparent boundaries, and explicit disclaimers regarding the limits of support.

endorsements.title: Mental Health Innovation Is Scaling Faster Than Accountability
endorsements.quote: Low-risk wellness tools may require clear scope limitations, privacy safeguards, user reporting channels, and disclosure that the tool is not a substitute for professional care.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether a written statement of an AI tool's intended purposes, population, abilities, and limitations reduces misuse or overreliance, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. Support for R076 rests on one state statute, one assurance framework, one guidance document, and three commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The six endorsements are expert opinion and policy text, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures user understanding or out-of-scope use with and without such statements.

Utah HB 452 (2025) is the only mandatory source, and the quoted clause requires development and monitoring consistent with clinical best practices rather than a written scope statement. The CHAI guide and the augmented intelligence principles use should language. Organizations may therefore face voluntary expectations more often than binding duties for this specific disclosure.

Three mental health commentaries ask that users be told what a tool cannot do, such as the absence of real-time clinician monitoring or crisis intervention, and that it does not replace professional care. These sources suggest patients value knowing when to seek a human, though none measured whether disclosure changed patient behavior.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare user comprehension, out-of-scope use, and escalation to human care between deployments that provide a written scope and limitations statement and those that do not, with attention to format, reading level, and timing of the statement.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether written statements work for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. A written format may reach these groups less well, and any future test should include translated and plain-language versions.
